ab1: I'm interested in what happens to a language when everyone speaks about it except the people who speak it.
ab2: I'm a student at the Faculty of International Relations, BSU, studying Africa and reading sources in French and Arabic — the languages the region is discussed in from outside. Hence my interest in what is said from inside, and how it gets written down.
ab3: I take research work and turn it into something people finish reading.
f1d: A difficult subject laid out so a reader without special training can follow it.
f2d: I read the paper in full, check the conclusions and explain what it actually shows.
f3d: A conversation with a researcher or a speaker of the language — in Russian, English or French.
f4d: The whole picture: who is working on what, where the argument is, and what is still unresolved.
f5d: A first-person piece for when a subject has a clear position worth naming.
fv1: BSU, Faculty of International Relations — African studies
fv4: Language policy, writing systems and manuscripts, NLP for low-resource languages, field linguistics
h1: I write about Africa through its languages
lede: I read sources in English, French and Arabic, and write about what is happening to the languages of the continent — from manuscripts to machine translation.
manifesto: Two thousand languages. Almost everything written about them is written by people who can't read the sources.
q1: From English, French and Arabic into Russian. From Russian into English.
q2: Research articles and book chapters · abstracts and conference papers · grant applications · project reports
q3: The humanities and social sciences: linguistics, anthropology, sociology, African studies, history, language policy.
q4: I check terminology against the sources and flag anything contested for discussion with the author.
